\chapter{Numbers One to Ten}
\label{ch:numbers-1-10}
\hlchaptermodality{6}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count from one to ten in French and use the numbers in a short exchange.}

The ten most-reused words in the language, taken one at a time. Each is a Latin numeral that barely moved on its way into French, so English has already handed you half of them — and four of them left a copy of themselves in the calendar, still counting two months out of place.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[un]{un — one}

\label{lesson:FR-C06-un}



\begin{quote}
Numbers are the most-reused words in any language, and French inherited them from Latin almost unchanged. You already half-know them through English. We take them \textbf{one at a time}, starting with the first.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{nasal-un} — \textbf{un} is a \textbf{nasal vowel}, close to \textquotedblleft{}uh\textquotedblright{} hummed through the nose. No \emph{n} is ever pronounced. The letters \emph{u-n} are a single sound, not two.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{un} (1) comes from Latin \textbf{ūnus}, and that root is everywhere in English:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{unit} — one thing counted
  \item \textbf{union} — many made one
  \item \textbf{unique} — one of its kind
  \item \textbf{universe} — everything turned into one
\end{itemize}

English \textbf{one} and \textbf{a/an} descend from the same ancient word, worn down at home rather than borrowed. Spanish keeps the Latin shape more plainly: \emph{uno}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one word for \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}}]
French draws no line between \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}a/an.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{un} does both jobs, and it takes the gender of the noun it stands in front of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{un} before a masculine noun — \emph{un jour}, \textquotedblleft{}a day\textquotedblright{} \textbf{or} \textquotedblleft{}one day\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{une} before a feminine noun — \emph{une nuit}, \textquotedblleft{}a night\textquotedblright{} \textbf{or} \textquotedblleft{}one night\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

You met that same masculine/feminine split in \emph{le} and \emph{la}. It is the same split, on a different word. Spanish does exactly this too (\emph{un} / \emph{una}). The counting words that follow never change shape; this first one is the only one that does.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}un\textquotedblright{} — hum it through the nose, no \emph{n} at the end
  \item \textquotedblleft{}un jour\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}une nuit\textquotedblright{} — same word, two genders
  \item \textquotedblleft{}un\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}unit, union, unique\textquotedblright{} — hear the ūnus
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say one in French? (\textbf{un}, nasal, with no \emph{n} sounded.) What two things does it mean? (\textbf{One}, and \textbf{a/an}.) What is its feminine form, and when do you use it? (\textbf{une}, before a feminine noun — \emph{une nuit}.) Next: the number two.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[deux]{deux — two}

\label{lesson:FR-C06-deux}



\begin{quote}
One down. The second number brings a vowel your mouth has to be taught, and a final letter you must \textbf{not} say.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-eu} — say \textquotedblleft{}eh,\textquotedblright{} then round your lips as if for \textquotedblleft{}oo\textquotedblright{} without moving your tongue. That rounded \emph{eu} is the whole word: \textbf{deux} = \emph{deuh}.
  \item \texttt{silent-final} — the \textbf{x} is silent. French writes letters at the end of a word that it has stopped pronouncing, and this is your first one.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{deux} (2) comes from Latin \textbf{duo}, which English borrowed several times over:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{duo} — two performers
  \item \textbf{dual}, \textbf{duel} — of two
  \item \textbf{duet} — a piece for two
  \item \textbf{double} — Latin \emph{duplus}, \textquotedblleft{}two-fold\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

Spanish went the other way with the same word and wore it down to \emph{dos}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}deux\textquotedblright{} — round the lips, stop before the \emph{x}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}un, deux\textquotedblright{} — count what you have so far
  \item \textquotedblleft{}deux jours\textquotedblright{} — two days
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say two? (\textbf{deux}, \emph{deuh}.) What happens to the \textbf{x}? (Nothing — it is silent.) Which English words carry the same Latin \emph{duo}? (\emph{Duo, dual, duet, double}.) Count what you have. (\emph{Un, deux}.) Next: the number three.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[trois]{trois — three}

\label{lesson:FR-C06-trois}



\begin{quote}
The third number shows you the most French vowel spelling there is: \textbf{oi}, which sounds nothing like either letter in it.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-oi} — the pair \textbf{oi} is always \emph{wa}. So \textbf{trois} = \emph{trwa}.
  \item \texttt{silent-final} — the \textbf{s} is silent here, exactly as the \emph{x} was in \emph{deux}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{trois} (3) comes from Latin \textbf{trēs}. Look at what happened next: French turned it into \emph{trois} and Spanish into \emph{tres}. \textbf{Same Roman word, worn two different ways} — the clearest picture yet of how one language becomes two.

English took the Latin form whole, over and over:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{trio} — three players
  \item \textbf{triple} — three-fold
  \item \textbf{trident} — three teeth
  \item \textbf{triangle} — three corners
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}trois\textquotedblright{} — \emph{trwa}, one syllable
  \item \textquotedblleft{}un, deux, trois\textquotedblright{} — the count so far
  \item \textquotedblleft{}trois\textquotedblright{} then Spanish \textquotedblleft{}tres\textquotedblright{} — one Latin word, two shapes
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say three? (\textbf{trois}, \emph{trwa}.) What sound does \textbf{oi} always make? (\emph{Wa}.) Which Latin word gave both \emph{trois} and Spanish \emph{tres}? (\textbf{trēs}.) Count to three. (\emph{Un, deux, trois}.) Next: the number four.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[quatre]{quatre — four}

\label{lesson:FR-C06-quatre}



\begin{quote}
The fourth number is the first that runs to two syllables, and it ends in a letter French writes but barely breathes.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{quatre} = \emph{KA-truh}. The \textbf{qu-} is a plain \emph{k}; no \emph{w} sound survives.
  \item \texttt{silent-final-e} — the closing \textbf{-e} is a whisper, not a vowel you lean on.
  \item \texttt{r-uvular} — the French \textbf{r} is made at the back of the throat, near where you would gargle, and never rolled at the tip of the tongue.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{quatre} (4) comes from Latin \textbf{quattuor}. English borrowed the Latin stem and kept the \emph{qua-} visible in every one:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{quart} — a fourth of a gallon
  \item \textbf{quarter} — a fourth of anything
  \item \textbf{quatrain} — a four-line verse
  \item \textbf{quadrant} — a quarter of a circle
\end{itemize}

Spanish stayed nearer the Latin with \emph{cuatro}; French compressed the middle of the word away.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}quatre\textquotedblright{} — \emph{KA-truh}, the \emph{r} at the back of the throat
  \item \textquotedblleft{}un, deux, trois, quatre\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}quatre\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}quarter, quadrant\textquotedblright{} — the same \emph{quattuor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say four? (\textbf{quatre}, \emph{KA-truh}.) Where in your mouth is the French \textbf{r} made? (At the \textbf{back of the throat}.) Which English words come from \emph{quattuor}? (\emph{Quart, quarter, quatrain, quadrant}.) Next: the number five, which closes the first hand.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cinq]{cinq — five}

\label{lesson:FR-C06-cinq}



\begin{quote}
Five closes the first hand — and this one came into English so completely that you have handled it on a pair of dice.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{soft-c-s} — a \textbf{c} before \emph{i} or \emph{e} is an \emph{s}. So \textbf{cinq} opens with \emph{s}, not \emph{k}.
  \item \texttt{nasal-in} — the \textbf{in} is nasal, like the \emph{un} you met in \textbf{un}, but with the tongue further forward. The \textbf{q} at the end \textbf{is} sounded: \emph{sank}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{cinq} (5) comes from Latin \textbf{quīnque}. English took the Latin stem for counting words:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{quintet} — five players
  \item \textbf{quintessence} — the \emph{fifth} essence, the one the ancients set above earth, water, air and fire
\end{itemize}

And English took the \textbf{French} word whole for one job: \textbf{cinque}, the five on a die or a playing card. Spanish, again, kept the Latin \emph{q}: \emph{cinco}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what the first five have in common}]
Set the five beside their Latin parents and one fact stands out: \textbf{the numbers barely moved.} \emph{ūnus, duo, trēs, quattuor, quīnque} went into French as the five words you have learned, and into Spanish as \emph{uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco}. Words used every day by every speaker are the words a language changes least.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}cinq\textquotedblright{} — \emph{sank}, the \emph{q} sounded
  \item \textquotedblleft{}un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq\textquotedblright{} — count the whole hand
  \item \textquotedblleft{}cinq jours\textquotedblright{} — five days
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say five? (\textbf{cinq}, \emph{sank}.) Why does the \textbf{c} sound like \emph{s}? (It stands before \textbf{i}.) Which English word for the 5 on a die is French? (\textbf{cinque}.) Count to five. (\emph{Un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq}.) Next: the number six, and a rule about final letters that turn on and off.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[six]{six — six}

\label{lesson:FR-C06-six}



\begin{quote}
Six is spelled like the English word and means the same thing. The new thing here is not the word. It is that its last sound \textbf{switches on and off} depending on what follows.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Counting on its own, \textbf{six} ends in an \emph{s} sound: \emph{sees}.
  \item The \textbf{i} is the short, tight vowel of English \emph{machine}, not of \emph{sit}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a final letter that comes and goes}]
French final consonants are not a fixed yes or no. \textbf{six} has three settings, and which one you hear is decided by the next word:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{counting, or standing alone} — the \emph{s} is sounded: \emph{sees}
  \item \textbf{before a consonant} — the \emph{s} falls silent: \emph{six livres} = \emph{see livres}
  \item \textbf{before a vowel} — it comes back voiced, as a \emph{z}: \emph{six ans} = \emph{see-\textbf{z}-ans}
\end{itemize}

That third case is called \textbf{liaison}: a silent ending waking up to bridge into a vowel. French does this constantly, and you will meet it in every chapter from here on.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{six} (6) comes from Latin \textbf{sex}, which is where English got:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{sextet} — six players
  \item \textbf{sextant} — an instrument marking a sixth of a circle
  \item \textbf{semester} — Latin \emph{sex mensis}, \textquotedblleft{}six months\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

Spanish made \emph{seis} from the same \emph{sex}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}six\textquotedblright{} alone — \emph{sees}, the \emph{s} sounded
  \item \textquotedblleft{}six livres\textquotedblright{} — \emph{see livres}, the \emph{s} gone
  \item the count so far, one through six
  \item \textquotedblleft{}six ans\textquotedblright{} — \emph{see-z-ans}, the \emph{s} back as a \emph{z}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say six when counting? (\emph{Sees}, with the \emph{s}.) What happens to that \emph{s} before a consonant? (It \textbf{goes silent} — \emph{six livres}.) And before a vowel? (It returns as a \textbf{z} — \emph{six ans}. That is \textbf{liaison}.) Next: the number seven, and a secret hidden in the calendar.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sept]{sept — seven}

\label{lesson:FR-C06-sept}



\begin{quote}
Seven is the first of four numbers that left a copy of themselves in the calendar. Learn the number and you have been handed a month.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{sept} = \emph{set}. The \textbf{p} is written and never spoken.
  \item The final \textbf{t}, unusually, \textbf{is} spoken. French keeps a handful of final consonants alive, and this is one of them.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sept} (7) comes from Latin \textbf{septem}. The same \emph{septem} stands, undisguised, at the front of a month you already know:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{septembre} — French for September
  \item \textbf{septet} — seven players
\end{itemize}

The month is worth staring at. \emph{Septembre} announces itself as the \textbf{seventh}, and everybody uses it as the ninth. That gap has an explanation, and it is waiting at the end of this chapter. Spanish made \emph{siete} from the same \emph{septem}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sept\textquotedblright{} — \emph{set}, no \emph{p}
  \item the count so far, one through seven
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sept\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}septembre\textquotedblright{} — the seven inside the month
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say seven? (\textbf{sept}, \emph{set}.) Which written letter is silent? (The \textbf{p}.) Which month carries the same Latin \emph{septem}? (\textbf{Septembre} — which is the ninth month, for a reason we come to.) Next: the number eight.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[huit]{huit — eight}

\label{lesson:FR-C06-huit}



\begin{quote}
Every number so far has looked like its Latin parent. This one looks like nothing at all — and that is the lesson.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{silent-h} — French never pronounces a written \textbf{h}. Not here, not anywhere.
  \item \textbf{huit} = \emph{weet}, with the final \textbf{t} sounded.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{huit} (8) comes from Latin \textbf{octō}, and the road it travelled is worth following step by step:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{octō} $\to$ \emph{oit} $\to$ \textbf{huit}
\end{quote}

The \emph{c} dropped out, the vowels softened, and a written \emph{h} grew on the front as a prop. The number came out unrecognisable. English, which borrowed the Latin form directly, kept it whole in \textbf{octave}, \textbf{octagon} and \textbf{octopus} — the eight-armed one.

Here is the consolation: French kept the old shape in the \textbf{month}. \textbf{Octobre} still carries \emph{oct-} in plain sight. The eight vanished from the number and survived in the calendar. Spanish made \emph{ocho}, which sits about halfway along the same road.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}huit\textquotedblright{} — \emph{weet}, no \emph{h}, with the \emph{t}
  \item the count so far, one through eight
  \item the road — \textquotedblleft{}octō, oit, huit\textquotedblright{} — then \textquotedblleft{}octobre\textquotedblright{}, where the \emph{oct-} held
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say eight? (\textbf{huit}, \emph{weet}.) What does French do with a written \textbf{h}? (Never pronounces it.) Which Latin word is \emph{huit} worn down from, and where can you still see it? (\textbf{octō} — kept intact in \textbf{octobre}.) Next: the number nine.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[neuf]{neuf — nine}

\label{lesson:FR-C06-neuf}



\begin{quote}
You met a final letter that goes silent before a consonant. Nine shows you the other move: a final letter that \textbf{changes shape} to reach a vowel.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{neuf} = \emph{nuhf}. The vowel is the rounded \emph{eu} you learned in \textbf{deux}, and the \textbf{f} is sounded.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the f that turns into a v}]
Standing before a vowel, the \textbf{f} of \emph{neuf} softens into a \textbf{v}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{neuf ans} (\textquotedblleft{}nine years\textquotedblright{}) = \emph{neu-\textbf{v}-ans}
  \item \textbf{neuf heures} (\textquotedblleft{}nine o'clock\textquotedblright{}) = \emph{neu-\textbf{v}-eures}
\end{itemize}

This is the same instinct you saw in \emph{six ans}: French will not let a consonant sit awkwardly against a following vowel, so it bends the sound to bridge them. With \emph{six} the ending woke up as a \emph{z}; with \emph{neuf} it softens to a \emph{v}. Both are liaison, doing the one job of keeping the line smooth.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{neuf} (9) comes from Latin \textbf{novem}. Once again the month kept the number visible: \textbf{novembre} wears its \emph{nov-} on the outside, and English has \textbf{novena}, a devotion of nine days. Spanish made \emph{nueve}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}neuf\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nuhf}, with the \emph{f}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}neuf ans\textquotedblright{} — \emph{neu-v-ans}, the \emph{f} softened
  \item \textquotedblleft{}six ans, neuf ans\textquotedblright{} — a \emph{z} and a \emph{v}, the same bridging move
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say nine? (\textbf{neuf}, \emph{nuhf}.) What happens to the \textbf{f} before a vowel? (It becomes a \textbf{v} — \emph{neuf ans}.) Which month keeps the same Latin \emph{novem}? (\textbf{Novembre}.) Next: the number ten, and the count is complete.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dix]{dix — ten}

\label{lesson:FR-C06-dix}



\begin{quote}
The last number of the count, and the one you have been carrying in your pocket in English without knowing it.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Counting on its own, \textbf{dix} ends in an \emph{s} sound: \emph{dees}.
  \item It behaves exactly like \textbf{six}: silent before a consonant (\emph{dix livres} = \emph{dee livres}), and back as a \emph{z} before a vowel (\emph{dix ans} = \emph{dee-\textbf{z}-ans}).
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dix} (10) comes from Latin \textbf{decem}, and it has left tracks in three places you already walk:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{décembre} — the month that says \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{decimal} — counting by tens
  \item \textbf{dime} — a tenth of a dollar. That one came through Old French \textbf{disme}, from Latin \emph{decima}, \textquotedblleft{}a tenth.\textquotedblright{} The coin in an American pocket is a French word for a tenth part.
\end{itemize}

Spanish made \emph{diez} from the same \emph{decem}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dix\textquotedblright{} alone — \emph{dees}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dix livres\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}dix ans\textquotedblright{} — silent, then \emph{z}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dix\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}decimal, dime\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{decem} in both
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say ten on its own? (\textbf{dix}, \emph{dees}.) Which other number shares its on-and-off ending? (\textbf{six}.) Which American coin is a worn-down French word for a tenth? (The \textbf{dime}, from \emph{disme} $\leftarrow$ \emph{decima}.) Next: why those four months are counting wrong.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[septembre, octobre, novembre, décembre]{The months that are off by two}

\label{lesson:FR-C06-mois-romains}



\begin{quote}
Four times in this chapter a number turned up at the front of a month, and four times the arithmetic was wrong by two. Here is why.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Line up what the four months \textbf{say} against where they \textbf{sit}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{month} & \textbf{says} & \textbf{sits at} \\
\midrule
\textbf{septembre} & seven (\emph{septem}) & 9th \\
\textbf{octobre} & eight (\emph{octō}) & 10th \\
\textbf{novembre} & nine (\emph{novem}) & 11th \\
\textbf{décembre} & ten (\emph{decem}) & 12th \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every one is two places late, and all four are late by the \textbf{same} two places. A single event moved them.

The old Roman year began in \textbf{March}, not January. Counting from March, \emph{September} genuinely was the seventh month and \emph{December} the tenth — the names were accurate. Later, two months named for two rulers, \textbf{juillet} (Julius) and \textbf{août} (Augustus), were fixed into the middle of the year, and the start of the year was moved back to January. The counting months were shoved two places along. Their Latin names never caught up.

So every December, in French and in English alike, you are saying the Roman word for \textbf{ten}. Spanish carries the identical fault: \emph{diciembre} is \emph{decem} too.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{septembre} mean, and which month is it? (\textbf{Seven} — and it is the ninth.) In which month did the old Roman year begin? (\textbf{March}.) Which two months were pushed in, and for whom? (\textbf{Juillet} and \textbf{août}, for Julius and Augustus.) What number are you saying when you say \emph{décembre}? (\textbf{Ten}, Latin \emph{decem}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — counting to ten, out loud and in use}

\label{lesson:FR-C06-practice}



\begin{quote}
Ten words, taken one at a time. Now run them together until the chain is one motion, then put it to work.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: the whole count}
Up, then down:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix}
\end{quote}

\emph{Twice through:} the count from one to ten

Then backwards, which is where a memorised chant stops helping and the words have to be individually yours: \emph{dix, neuf, huit, sept, six, cinq, quatre, trois, deux, un}.

\subsection*{Your turn: the endings that move}
Three numbers change sound depending on what comes next. Say each pair and listen for the difference:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{six livres} / \emph{six ans} — silent, then \textbf{z}
  \item \emph{dix livres} / \emph{dix ans} — silent, then \textbf{z}
  \item \emph{neuf livres} / \emph{neuf ans} — \textbf{f}, then \textbf{v}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: say something real}
\begin{quote}
— Bonjour ! \textbf{Un} jour ? — Non, \textbf{deux} jours.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{Trois} ? — Non, \textbf{deux}. Merci !
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
— De rien. Bonne nuit — \textbf{une} nuit, \textbf{deux} nuits.
\end{quote}

Say how many, then correct yourself. The exchange is short on purpose: every word in it is already yours, from this chapter or from the first.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{un} to \textbf{dix} — the ten most-reused words in the language, each of them a Latin numeral that barely moved on the way in.
  \item \textbf{un / une} — the number one doubling as \textquotedblleft{}a/an,\textquotedblright{} and taking gender.
  \item \textbf{liaison} — \emph{six}, \emph{dix} and \emph{neuf} changing their final sound to reach a following vowel.
  \item \textbf{septembre} to \textbf{décembre} — four months still counting seven to ten, two places out of place ever since the Roman year stopped starting in March.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count from one to ten without stopping. Now backwards. Which three numbers change their ending before a vowel, and how? (\emph{Six} and \emph{dix} to a \textbf{z}, \emph{neuf} to a \textbf{v}.) What is the difference between \emph{un jour} and \emph{une nuit}? (Gender — the same word for \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}a,\textquotedblright{} agreeing with the noun.) Why is \emph{décembre} the twelfth month when it says ten? (The Roman year began in \textbf{March}, and two months were inserted.)
\end{tcolorbox}
